subtopic: AMENDMENT TO REMOVE DISQUALIFICATION OF INMATES OF INSTITUTIONS FOR THE POOR

subtopic: AMENDMENT TO REMOVE DISQUALIFICATION OF INMATES OF INSTITUTIONS FOR THE POOR
speechtext:
This amendment is designed to remove the disqualification imposed on inmates of institutions for the poor where such persons are disqualified from voting at a provincial election. The removal of this disqualification will enable all such worthy persons to vote and also remove the existing anomaly of such persons being qualified to vote in some provinces and disqualified in other provinces.

Mr. Speaker, on Friday last, subsequent to the statement of the Prime Minister on the government's policy on domestic and international aviation, I asked him if he would indicate when he expected the negotiations between the various nations on this subject to begin, and also if he would indicate whether or not there had -been any preliminary discussions on the subject between the united nations and others who might be involved. At that time the Prime Minister answered that he was not in a position to indicate when negotiations would be formally commenced between the united nations, but with regard to the point raised as to preliminary discussions, he asked that my question stand as a notice, so that more exact information might be given at another time. I should like to ask the Prime Minister if he is now in a position tp inform the house of the, nature and extent of the preliminary discussions, if any, which did take place, prior to his making
[Mr. Ralston.!
the announcement to which I have referred, and also if there have been since any formal or informal communications or discussions between any other nation and Canada with respect to the subjects dealt with in his announcement, and if so, the nature of such communications.

speakeroldname: Right Hon. W. L. MACKENZIE KING (Prime Minister):
speakerposition: Prime Minister; Secretary of State for External Affairs; President of the Privy Council
maintopic: QUESTIONS PASSED AS ORDERS FOR RETURNS
subtopic: CIVIL AIR TRANSPORT
subsubtopic: STATEMENT WITH RESPECT TO POLICY AS TO DOMESTIC AND INTERNATIONAL AVIATION
speechtext:
Mr, Speaker, my hon. friend will see from the statement I have in my hand that I had intended to answer his question to-day. I would answer it in this way.
Some aspects of the problems of international air transport after the war have already been the subject of informal discussions with the other governments most directly concerned. The general problem raises broad questions of principle which affect all the united nations, and it may be expected that in due course we shall be exchanging views with them.
In the statement I have just made there is reference to informal discussions with other governments.
On a previous occasion in this house, on March 10, a question was asked as to whether talks had taken place between Canada and the United States concerning post-war civil aviation. I replied:
In the frequent discussions which take place between officers of the Canadian Legation in Washington and officers of the State Department on questions of common concern, reference has been made to the problems of post-war civil aviation.
I might add that in a statement made on March, 11 in the British House of Commons by the Secretary of State for Air, Sir Archibald Sinclair said:
None of the arrangements we have made during the war with regard to air transport in any part of the world precludes us from working out new plans. Our exploration work is, in fact, in hand and we are now in preliminary consultation with the dominions and with India. Consultations with other members of the united nations will follow.
The consultation there referred to was two or three meetings that were called of the high commissioners in London at which certain matters of air transportation were communicated by the British government to our high commissioners for their information and transmitted by them to their respective governments. That covers I think all that I am in a position to say on the matter at the present time.

Men who are in essential industry are granted postponement from military service because they are essential to agriculture. subtopic: INQUIRY WITH RESPECT TO DEBT ADJUSTMENT LEGISLATION
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, in connection with the necessity for early action concerning debt adjustment legislation, I would ask the Minister of Justice whether or not a decision has been made with respect to debt adjustment, and whether legislation will be introduced before the Easter recess.
Hon. L. S. ST. LAURENT (Minister of Justice): This matter has been raised in the house before, and I said then I was not in a position to make a statement. I need not say that the matter has been receiving very earnest consideration.
At this time, however, I can say that in February, 1943, the privy council held the Alberta debt adjustment act to be ultra vires because it was in relation to bankruptcy and insolvency, mainly for the reasons that the statute was designed to compel compositions and prevented enforcement of claims so that there could be no "debt owing" within the meaning of the Bankruptcy Act. As all hon. members know, on the other hand it had been held that the Farmers' Creditors Arrangement Act is valid legislation within the jurisdiction of the federal parliament, but it is 
clear that this jurisdiction is confined to parliament's right to legislate in respect to bankruptcy and insolvency.
A bill to amend this act is being prepared to make it a more effective instrument and to extend its application to Manitoba as well as Saskatchewan and Alberta, but it is not probable that this bill can be introduced, and it certainly could not be enacted, before the Easter recess.
While the jurisdiction of parliament is ordinarily limited to bankruptcy and insolvency, it is felt that as a war measure provision might be made to maintain, for the duration of the war, the production, of foodstuffs, and to that end keep on the land in the western provinces every farmer who is an efficient food producer. It is therefore intended to enact by order in council a provision somewhat similar in purpose and effect to the provision contained in section 15 of the Saskatchewan statute, "The Limitation of Civil Rights Act."
It may be noted that this provision was first enacted in Saskatchewan in 1939, and is designed to enable the court in an action for the recovery of land (foreclosure, sale, specific performance, rescission of agreement or possession of land), to make an order for the temporary relief of the debtor.
Subsection 1 of section 15 aforesaid provides as follows:
15. (1) In an action:
(a)	By a mortgagee, or his personal representatives or assigns, for foreclosure of the equity of redemption, or for sale or possession of the mortgaged premises or for the recovery of any moneys payable under the mortgage;
(b)	by a vendor of ^ land, or his personal representatives or assigns, for specific performance or cancellation of an agreement for sale of land, or for sale or possession of land sold under agreement of sale;
_ The court or judge may, after making such inquiries as are deemed necessary concerning the income and assets of the parties and all other matters which may appear relevant, grant or refuse to grant any order, stay the action, postpone payment of any moneys due, prescribe terms and conditions to which any order shall be subject, vary or extend any order from time to time, and give any direction as to costs; and in disposing of any application the court or judge shall have and exercise discretion in each case and shall act upon its or his own view of the proper order to be made having regard to all the facts and notwithstanding any order or ruling heretofore made at any time in any other action.

speechtext:
A report appeared in the press last week which I should like to bring to the notice of the house. This report appeared in the Ottawa Citizen of April 1 last.
New "authority" to guide affairs seen by Sandwell.
A "supranational authority" with power to settle questions of immigration, natural resources, treatment of minorities, repudiation of debts, finance and other questions was predicted by B. K. Sandwell of Toronto in an address before the Ottawa branch of the League of Nations Society last evening in the railway committee room of the senate.
To bring about Canada's acceptance of the new "authority" however, Mr. Sandwell said it would be necessary to bring all the people to a diminution of their loyalty of the crown by substituting a new loyalty to an "authority wider than Canada, than the British commonwealth of nations, and the United States or all the democracies together ..."
Mr. Sandwell said-
. . . it is up to such organizations as the league-to endeavour to develop among Canadians "the will to sacrifice a substantial part of their national rights" for this new "authority".
I should like to ask the government, or perhaps the Minister of Justice (Mr. St. Laurent) whether it does not constitute sedition, especially perhaps at this time, for a man to make statements to the effect that Canadians, British subjects, must renounce their loyalty to the crown, as to which every hon. member of this house has taken his oath before taking his seat in the house.

I think the hon. member might have gone further, had his voice permitted, and brought to the attention of the Minister of Justice and of this house the fact that there are dangerous forces at work, sometimes not appearing in the open, that would attempt to destroy the sovereignty of the British crown. I am surprised that the traditional Conservative party in Canada have not been alive to this situation. Perhaps they have become so "progressive" they have forgotten that sometimes the traditional aspect of Conservatism has some value. It does seem strange to me, Mr. Speaker, that *on the very day Mr. Eden was speaking to us in this house, the very day that the Prime Minister of Canada should send by Mr. Eden to Their Majesties the felicitations of Canada, within this very building, in a certain committee room, there should appear before the hon. gentlemen who usually sit in another place a speaker who would give an address such as is recorded in the press dispatch appearing in the Ottawa Citizen of April 1.

. . . it would be necessary to bring all the people to a diminution of their loyalty to the crown by substituting a new loyalty to an ' authority wider than Canada, than the British commonwealth of nations and the United States or all the democracies together and might even become wide enough to enfold the whole human race."
And further:
"Even while the world is being administered by these four nations-
I suppose he means the united nations.
-the peoples of Canada, Australia and other countries will be preparing for a more constituted structure of affairs," Mr. Sandwell declared, saying that it was up to such organizations as the league-
He was speaking to the League of Nations Society.

to endeavour to develop among Canadians "the will to sacrifice a substantial part of their national rights" for this new "authority."
One thing the Canadian forces are fighting for is the traditional principles for which the British commonwealth of nations has always stood. One thing for which we are fighting is the preservation of the sovereignty of the British crown. Let it go on the record now- the Conservative party can put itself on record also if it wishes-that there is one thing for which social creditors stand. You can call them funny money men, if you like; you can call them crackpots, if you like, but there is one thing for which they stand, and that is the sovereignty of the crown of England. We become tremendously alarmed when we recognize that there are forces working for the destruction of the crown. I am not so much concerned with or alarmed at Mr. Sandwell

saying this. I have never met this gentleman, but in my view he is voicing the same opinions that have been expressed by much greater authorities than he, and it is time this house became alive to and alarmed at the situation which exists. If we win this war, as we will, but lose in the peace the authority now vested in the crown, then we shall have fought this war in vain.

I want to say to him that I have no more confidence in the gold standard than he has, but as nations move forward in the days to come it is certain that if we are to preserve law and order in the world, if we are to escape these recurrent wars, then every nation must abide by an international code of law and no nation can usurp the rights of other people by making war against the world. I notice that Mr. Churchill stood for collective security. A man who spoke here a week ago to-morrow, Mr. Anthony Eden, has throughout his public career stood for collective security and the organization of nations to prevent war. I could mention also Mr. Herbert Morrison, Sir Stafford Cripps, and [DOT]others who are members of the British war cabinet, men of all sorts and conditions who stand for collective security as opposed to world anarchy.
I do not want to prolong the discussion. I simply wanted to say that as a member of the League of Nations Society in Canada, as a member of the national executive, I am proud to be associated with that group of men and women who are intensely loyal to Canada and to the sovereign of Canada.

speechtext:
Mr. *Speaker, the years from 1918 to the outbreak

of this war were the most disastrous in the history of civilization. My hon. friends to my left and others believed that we could depend on peace pacts, on Kellogg notes and Locarno notes and all that sort of thing for our defence. The result was that Britain threw away the greatest army, the greatest navy and the greatest air force the world had ever seen. It was these pacifists and internationalists that got us into this war. Now they are up to their old game even though this war has not been won. The only collective security the world ever had was Great Britain and' the British fleet. That is the only league of nations that was ever a success-the British empire and all it stands for down the ages.
There have been these leagues before. They had them in the days of the Romans, but there was always the same result. The pacifists almost caused the destruction of civilization in this war. They are still up to their old tricks. The writer of the article referred to was one of those who went up and down this country saying that we did not need any army, any navy or any air force; that we could depend on the league and collective security. That was a thing of the past; we were to depend on collective security. There is no such thing, and there can be no collective security unless the war is won. These hon. gentlemen who bring this matter before us to-day have been wrong before. They were wrong for the twenty years between the two great wars. They would disband our army, navy and air force. Ramsay MacDonald went up and down the country preaching pacifism. He was under observation during the last war. If he had had his way, we would have lost it. Right in the city of Ottawa to-day there is an exhibition being put on by the navy league; if similar leagues to oppose pacifism had been more active in the twenty years before this war we would not have had this second world war. Is it any wonder that we have a five billion dollar budget?
The League of Nations was the biggest farce and humbug the world ever saw. The pacifists and the league saw Germany arming from 1935 onwards, and they supported disarmament. What was the policy of these people in the old country who were supporting the league? They allowed Germany to rearm, and their pacifist policy caused this war. This dominion has spent nearly five million dollars of the taxpayers' money on a useless league of sham and humbug, because that is all it ever was. The pacifists blindfolded the people of the old country and led the politicians there to disarm. The

Address oj B. K. Sandwell
United States, which proposed the league, was led by the pacifists andi isolationists in that country to fade out of the league and leave Britain to go it all by itself. Russia and the United States came into the war when they were attacked. The result was that Britain entered the war alone, not because she was attacked, but because of an honourable pledge given to Poland. Look at the way Poland is suffering to-day. I referred in this house not long ago to the fact that one million Poles, men, women and helpless children, as a result of this league farce and the work they carried on, had been snatched from their homes and their work and taken to the abattoir to be treated by the Germans just as if they were a lot of animals and put to death. While the league was talking disarmament and writing notes, Germany went on rearming, and we were told that there would be no more war, that we could depend on pacifism, the Monroe doctrine, internationalism and all that kind of thing, and now the old game is being played over again. They are getting ready for a third world war. Just link yourselves up with the pacifists again and you will have another world war, and children who are babies to-day will be called out twenty years hence to fight in another world war because of this dream of a new world that is held by the pacifists. That has been tried before and failed.
I am opposed, Mr. Speaker, to holding up the business of the house by bringing before it academic matters of this kind when the Minister of Finance wishes to go into committee of ways and means. Evidently we shall have to change the rules of the house if we are to make any progress at all. Are we going to sit here day after day listening to academic discussions while our young men in Libya and Tunisia are fighting battles for SI.30 a day? We sit here day after day listening to academic discussions on domestic matters which hold up supply and prevent us from voting money for the men of our armed forces. If that continues they are going to insist on a showdown with the pacifists and internationalists when they come back home.
I can tell you this, that the people of this country are in no mood to spend another dollar on a farce like the League of Nations. The money that was voted and spent on the league was wasted and eventually led to this second war. They talk of collective social security and would secure peace by legislation. But we know how the German people have acted for the last two thousand years. The world had the same trouble with them in the days of the
Romans, and there was a league then. Read Gibbons "Decline and Fall of the Roman Empire" on doles and circuses, and Bryce's "History of the Holy Roman Empire", to see who it was that made the wars and bled the people of the world for centuries past.
Talk of freedom from fear! There can be no freedom from fear until Britain regains command of the seas. This war might go on for four or five or six years more. That is what it looks like-a seven years' war-while we sit here talking about a league that never had any right to exist. Britain has lost the command of the seas, and until she and the allies regain that command we can do nothing to invade the continent. It seems to me that we have had nothing but politics in this house for the last two years, the plebiscite last year, and all that kind of thing, and the same thing is going on this year. Our time is taken up with academic and political questions instead of being devoted to the war. This proposal of pacificism will not amount to a snap of the finger in defeating Hitler and the axis powers. We are as close to defeat now as we were when the war broke out. Germany to-day occupies practically the whole of Europe, and is in command of the coastline from Norway right down to Gibraltar.
Read what Mr. Knox said yesterday in the United States on the Atlantic problem. I venture to say that the isolationist party in the United States after this war will follow the policy of Woodrow Wilson and have nothing to do with the league or with foreign wars. These gentlemen were wrong before. They were wrong twenty years before this war, they are wrong again to-day. We have not got inside the German defences on the continent yet. The spring campaign is to open up soon, and here we are sitting in this house talking about matters of this kind. I say in all seriousness that this is no time to be talking of pacifist societies, and of everything but the war. They and the pacifist press and people who supported them have had their day. In the old country the government was advised by military experts during the years of peace to keep the army and navy and air force strong, but they would not do it. Then came the battle of Britain, and Britain was barely saved. After Dunkirk, if it had not been for the British fleet and the mother country, we would have had the Germans out on this continent and Washington and Ottawa would have had to seek peace long ago from the axis powers.
I am not responsible, Mr. Speaker, for the addresses that are being made here to-day. I protest against this practice of drawing a red herring across the track when we and our allies are fighting for our very lives for the right even to live. Why should we be wasting time
Address of B. K. Sandwell

to bring into effect somebody's pet theory aboui a new paradise that is to come when our young people who enlisted are fighting for their lives? Here we are wasting time discussing remedies and patent medicines with regard to domestic affairs, as if that were what we are fighting for-proposals that are made in this house and out of it to protect the public in the future-while the war is not yet won. We may have the axis powers out here before very long unless we do more than we have done already.
I deeply sympathize with the three ministers of defence and with the government. As an independent member of the house I have always supported any measure which would make our war effort more effective. I wish to encourage the government all I can to make ours a total war effort, and anything that the ministers in charge of the three defence departments do to bring that about will have my support and I believe the support of everyone in the opposition.
Again I protest against holding up the business of the house by bringing forward such matters as have been raised to-day. It is obvious that the rules of the house will have to be changed. Here is the Minister of Finance wanting to get into committee of ways and means with a five billion dollar budget, and the time of the house is wasted by bringing forward academic domestic matters. We should be devoting our energies to the war and eliminating everything else. Compare our proceedings here with how business is conducted at Westminster. There 99 per cent of the time of parliament is devoted to war measures. It is true that domestic measures are most important for the welfare of the men, women and children of this country, and I sympathize with my friends to my left in urging some of them, but they are only secondary. Here we have given away all our powers to outside boards and authorities. We have controllers and boards making expenditures without parliament hearing anything about them. Here we sit and talk about everything else but the war. The war is not far from our shores to-day.
I protest against the league and all connected with it. The president of the league got a job down in Chile. The best way to cure insomnia in the twenty years following the last war was to be connected with the league and to get a trip to Geneva and go there and listen to the babble of the pacifists. And what did the league do? They got Canada to pass sanctions against Italy, and then we quickly withdrew those sanctions. They threw away our defences as well as our friends.
IMr. Church.]
Through the league we lost two allies that we could have had when we entered this war. The people back home in the constituencies, when they get their tax bills, have no doubt about who caused the war. Let me say to the gentlemen who are banging their desks that they are responsible for the pacifism which brought about this second war. This same banging of desks went on for twenty years in this house when I was a lone voice crying in the wilderness, endeavouring to get a united House of Commons against pacifism and for rearmament. In fact, many on my own side of the house thought I was going too far when I would not support the league and all connected with it. I can say this, that in a very humble way I have done my duty as a member of parliament.
I protest against a discussion of this kind on the motion for committee of ways and means. The country cannot be carried on unless we have the money. I do not agree very often with the Minister of Finance (Mr. Ilsley), but he is a hard-working, conscientious official and does the best he can. He is not altogether responsible for the magnitude of the budget.
I do not blame those who got nice trips over to Geneva. They say the boats were comfortable; there were cigars and beverages; the meals were excellent, and everybody had a most enjoyable time. Indeed, a lady who used to be a member of this house, and for whom I have a great regard1, because she was a good member, wanted to have me sent over as a delegate to the league assembly, because, she said, I would be one of those who went over to scoff but would come back to pray for the success of the league and praise what it had done. However, her own opinions have changed entirely; she is going up and down the province of Ontario and at times is not as friendly to the league.
It is the people with views which I have described who caused the second world war; they were somewhat responsible for the first war; and before another twenty years have gone by there will probably be another war, with proposals for another league of North America and all that kind of thing. I can tell you this, I read every day in the Congressional Record the proceedings of the senate and congress at Washington, and I am convinced that after this war they are going to get right out of this international business and back to isolationism. That is the view of ninety per cent of the people. We should stop playing with great international issues along league lines, because it is a sheer waste of money. We threw away five million dollars on this venture, and what have we got? A second world war, with the prospect of another one

if leagues and internationalism are continued. These gentlemen have always been wrong. They were wrong about the first war; they were wrong in the twenty years which followed it; they are wrong about this war; and if they have their way, there will be a third war in another twenty years' time.

speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, this telegram came to me this morning, as I presume it did to the hon. member for Vancouver East (Mr. Maclnnis). Upon receiving it, I immediately got in touch with the Minister of Agriculture (Mr. Gardiner), and was assured by him that as soon as the facts arrived by airmail he would be more than pleased to give the matter consideration.
It will be noticed the telegram, as presented, is signed by five independent meat packers and processors. While it does not say who they are, the important thing is that the facts upon which their complaints are based are coming by airmail. They have not yet arrived this afternoon.
One of the difficulties hon. members are up against in these matters is that we are not made acquainted with all the orders issued by the wartime prices and trade board. I doubt very much if many of them would have much meaning to the average member, unless they were first explained by members of the trade to which they were directed.
It has been suggested that western members are not taking enough interest in this type of complaint. While I am on my feet may I point out that in the desire of those responsible for administration to secure greater efficiency 
there is always the danger of wiping out the little man, and depending upon the larger organizations which may be capable of producing better results, for the time being. I hope if there is anything in these charges they may be made the subject of a real inquiry, because it does seem to me the time has come when parliament may have to intervene to prevent what may become a steady drift toward one of the greatest dangers in a democracy, namely, the development of overriding and all-powerful monopolies throughout the trade and industry of our country.
The sacrifices we are called upon to make will have to be made. But at the same time wherever freedom of enterprise and freedom of trade can be maintained, without injury to the war effort, it should be done, as against a policy of monopolistic development.
I have nothing further to say, because I have not yet received the instructions. I can, however, assure my hon. friend that as soon as they arrive I, for one, will be more than pleased to associate myself with him or any other western members in having the matter properly presented to the minister in charge.

subtopic: MEAT INDUSTRY-ALLEGED DISCRIMINATION IN WARTIME PRICES AND BACON BOARD REGULATIONS
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, in my opinion this is a serious matter, and one which should be investigated by both the Minister of Agriculture (Mr. Gardiner) and the Minister of Finance (Mr. Usley). When Mr. Donald Gordon was in Vancouver in January he was interviewed by these independent meat packers, two of whom are the Alberta Meat Company and the Pacific Meat Company Limited. They laid their complaints before Mr. Gordon at that time and he assured them he would have an investigation made.
At that time two of the chief complaints were these:	In the first place, in 1942 west
coast packing plants had been ordered to reduce their hog killings to fifty per cent of the 1940 business. They say that meant to about twenty-five per cent of their 1941 business. One press report points out that a certain plant had to reduce weekly hog killings from 1,400 to about 350. Apparently the hogkilling end of the business was the only profitable part of it. They cannot make a profit in these times from beef killings.
The second complaint was that western packers were not allowed to participate in the export of bacon to Great Britain, and that this export trade was reserved1 to the eastern packers. Since there was a guaranteed price, set high enough for the eastern packers to make a good profit, western men said that the position was entirely unfair to them. They no doubt have the feeling that the large

Meat Industry
companies which have their main plants in the east, and only branches in the west, are making their profits out of business done in the east. And it is suggested that by making suggestions with regard to these orders they are, in effect, putting independent plants in the west out of business.
The present complaint has arisen as a result of the change made last week in prices of pork products. These packers claim that that is simply one more step toward having them wiped out, and they hold the view that the government is listening too much to the advice coming from large packing plants. I suggest to both ministers I have mentioned that the merits of the complaint must be carefully investigated and, as two other hon. members from Vancouver have done, I ask that the investigation be made promptly and thoroughly.

speakeroldname: Hon. J. G. GARDINER (Minister of Agriculture) :
subtopic: MEAT INDUSTRY-ALLEGED DISCRIMINATION IN WARTIME PRICES AND BACON BOARD REGULATIONS
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I believe I should say a word about one matter to which reference was made a moment ago. It is suggested that, because there is an agreement with Great Britain for the shipment of hogs from this country, the packing plants shipping that product, constituting about seventy per cent of the hogs slaughtered under inspection in Canada, are benefiting by that deal to the point where they are taking business away from some others who do not sell under the agreement.
May I say at once that the lowest price being obtained by any packing plants in Canada for pork products is the price obtained from Great Britain. As I recall the figures from memory, the situation in Vancouver arises from the fact that British Columbia produces only one-third of the hogs consumed in that city. Under ordinary circumstances this means that there is a local market in Vancouver for all hogs produced there. Hogs do cross the mountains into British Columbia, so that the slaughter of hogs in that province may be increased. That is a local market. Any local market in Canada to-day pays a much higher price for hogs than is paid under the British agreement.
Let me illustrate the point. The British agreement makes possible a price of about $11.20 at Winnipeg for live hogs. Anyone who has been following prices on the Winnipeg market knows that they have been away above that amount, ever since the British agreement was signed. The reason why they are away above is that all hogs sold locally in Canada bring a much higher price than the price under the agreement. So that a packer who is selling hogs under the British agreement is
not in a position to take profitable business away from those who do not sell under the agreement. I would be surprised to find any packer in Vancouver who would wish to sell hogs under the agreement. They have a special market, right at their own doors, a market which pays a higher price for pork than is provided under the agreement. Therefore I should expect they would want to keep that market, and sell in it.
The other question raised, with regard to any regulations that have been put into effect recently-

subtopic: MEAT INDUSTRY-ALLEGED DISCRIMINATION IN WARTIME PRICES AND BACON BOARD REGULATIONS
speechtext: Before the minister leaves the first question, will he say whether export bacon is receiving anything from the stabilization fund by way of subsidy?

subtopic: MEAT INDUSTRY-ALLEGED DISCRIMINATION IN WARTIME PRICES AND BACON BOARD REGULATIONS
speechtext: If it is, it is all beneath the price of which I am speaking. There is nothing over and above the price we are receiving from Britain under the agreement. That is the only return any packing house can get. We are selling bacon to Britain on the basis of 110 shillings, and the price to the packing house is under that price. That 110 shillings is what provides the $11.20 at Winnipeg. Anyone who is selling under that agreement to Britain is not getting as much for the pork product he is selling as he could get if he sold it all in Canada. Those who are selling all their pork products in Canada are getting a higher return than if they were selling under the British agreement.

subtopic: MEAT INDUSTRY-ALLEGED DISCRIMINATION IN WARTIME PRICES AND BACON BOARD REGULATIONS
speechtext: Would it be possible for a packing house that is selling in Britain and making a profit under that contract to raise the price of hogs for local consumption for the purpose of shutting out independent packers who are not making any profit out of the business with Britain? I understand that is the complaint.

subtopic: MEAT INDUSTRY-ALLEGED DISCRIMINATION IN WARTIME PRICES AND BACON BOARD REGULATIONS
speechtext:
I would not be in a position to answer that question offhand; there would have to be some inquiry made. But I know this, that in the first few months after the war started, as a result of an agreement entered into with Britain-I am speaking again from memory-I think some forty small packing houses that were not supplying bacon under the British agreement made handsome profits. And then, on account of conditions which developed in the spring of 1940 they were not able to make the same profit. A delegation came here at that time asking the government of Canada to see to it that some of the money which had been accumulated as a result of the activities in the early days of the agreement should be divided up among those particular packing plants. I might say that each

Mutual Aid-Administration Staff
time there has been a change in the agreement packing plants of different types, those who have been supplying to Britain or those who have not, have made representations to the government. There have been no representations in recent months; I would say there have been none in the last two years, from those plants that are not supplying under the British agreement to indicate that they are not doing just as well as any other plants.

subtopic: MEAT INDUSTRY-ALLEGED DISCRIMINATION IN WARTIME PRICES AND BACON BOARD REGULATIONS
speechtext: What about this representation to Donald Gordon?

subtopic: MEAT INDUSTRY-ALLEGED DISCRIMINATION IN WARTIME PRICES AND BACON BOARD REGULATIONS
speechtext:
These representations
being made now, in so far as they relate to the bacon board, are with regard to an attempt to get hogs into such plants as will make it possible to send a sufficient amount of bacon to Great Britain. The only plants that can supply bacon to Great Britain are those that are under government inspection, or in other words, plants the equipment of which measures up to the standards set by the department, standards which were set before the war started. Other plants which do not have that standard equipment, and therefore have not government inspection, do not supply the product under the British agreement. Only those plants that are up to the standard and have government inspection are supplying all the product, and there is only one way to get that product to Great Britain, namely, by putting it through plants that are subject to government inspection.
If someone in this country starts to set up a system under which they will take away a considerable part of the pork from those plants under any regulations that are set up, then someone will have to set up some other regulations to ensure that a sufficient amount of pork goes to plants where it can be properly processed to go to Britain, or no pork products will be going to the British market under our agreement. I do not doubt that some of the regulations which are put into effect are for the purpose of seeing to it that at least sufficient amounts of pork or a sufficient number of hogs get into properly inspected plants to make it possible to send that pork to Britain. That does not mean that they will make more money than those who are selling in Canada.

The wartime prices and trade board appears to come into this picture in some way, I do not know just how, probably as a result of a price order they have made. As soon as I have any facts I will investigate the matter and see whether there is anything wrong.

subtopic: REFERENCE TO QUESTION PASSED AS ORDER FOR RETURN-H.M.C.S. "CHIPPAWA"
speechtext:
The hon. gentleman has asked for unanimous consent, but unanimous consent has not been given; therefore he cannot place the table upon Hansard.
Motion agreed to and the house went into committee of ways and means, Mr. Bradette in the chair.

Resolved, that it is expedient to amend the Income War Tax Act and to provide:
1. That in respect of the taxation year 1942 the income tax liability, of taxpayers other than corporations, under subsection 1 of section 9 of the Income War Tax Act, in respect of earned income and in respect of investment income up to $3,000 shall be one-half of the amount calculated according to the schedules therein specified.

I
noticed in the press last week that employers must now give their employees a statement of income. I do not think the minister has said anything in regard to that. This press report states:
The revenue department ordered Friday that all employers, on or before May 31, must furnish each of their employees with a form showing the salary or wages paid to that employee during the preceding calendar year and the amount of tax deducted or withheld in respect of that salary or wage.
In subsequent years employers must furnish their employees with similar forms by the end of February.
On an employee leaving his job, the employer shall, if the employee requests, furnish the employee with a statement showing the amount of salary or wages paid to the date of cessation of the employee's job and the amount of tax deducted or withheld.
The order was published in the Canada Gazette.
When we were on the budget resolutions last year and, I believe, the year before I asked a number of questions as to what was being done in regard to those employees who did not have incomes of more than S660, if single, or SI ,200, if married, and I wonder if the employers will also have to send statements to their employees who have left their service, because there has been quite a transfer in various plants. Some men may have been in one plant the year before last and in another plant last year, or they may have been in one plant for only six months. Would the minister make a statement in regard to what has been done in respect of these men?

The regulation just read was recently instituted in order to ensure that each employee would be given information at each pay period as to the amount of deduction that had been made on account of the tax. In regard to the deductions made from employees who did not receive taxable incomes, namely, $660 a year, if single, or $1,200, if married, arrangements have been made to refund the amount of tax deducted in 1942. A special form has been prepared; the employee takes it to his employer and has the details of deductions filled in; then the employee completes the form himself, and a speedy refund is being made of the tax deducted last year.

Income War Tax
What does the minister mean by "speedy"? I know of some who have had requests for returns pending for the last eleven or twelve months.
Not in connection with these taxes deducted from people who were not taxable last year.
I am speaking of 1941, even.

There are two entirely different questions involved. In this case we are not waiting for the man to file an individual tax return; we are not calling upon him to file that return, which normally would not be filed until June of this year. We are accepting the statement by the employer that the man did not receive more than S660 or $1,200, and we are making the refund on the basis of that statement. These refunds will be made at once. In connection with the refunds for 1940-41, it has taken a considerable time to repay them, due to the fact that we have had gi'eat difficulty in increasing our income tax staff quickly enough to take care of them, but I understand that about ninety-five per cent of the refunds for 1940 have been made, as well as a very high percentage of the 1941 tax refunds, I think seventy-eight per cent.
The minister mentioned "each pay period", but this says, "at the end of the calendar year." That would be a definite statement which the employee would get at the end of the calendar year?

At the end of the calendar year the employer must notify the department. Before going further, I might explain that within a week after each pay period the employer must turn in to the department the money he has deducted on account of these taxes. He sends in the money, but he does not at that time give the department the names of the employees from whom it has been deducted. At the end of the year the employer sends to the department the names of the employees from whom deductions have been made, at the same time notifying each employee of the amount of tax which has been deducted during the year. In that way the employee is able to include these deductions on his return as a set-off against his individual tax.
What about the employee who has left that plant; what chance has he to get a statement of what he has paid in?

The employee, when he leaves, should apply to his employer for a statement, or he can write in and get the

statement from the employer at any time. The employee himself should ask for it from his employer, because otherwise, while the department would have the information, the employer might not know where to find the former employee.

Representing a taxpaying city which contributes a very large percentage of these income taxes, I wish to place before the committee the pattern of this pay-as-you-go plan. In my opinion the principle of paying the arrears of 1942 without further time allowed, is not fair to the small taxpayer with a fixed income. He has already made commitments in connection with real estate, insurance, mortgages and so on. How is he to pay the compound income tax, the balance of 1942 and the tax of 1943? It is too heavy a load1. I do not know how he can carry the burden. The farmers receive much better treatment. I have no objection to their getting all they can, but the fact is that they pay no income tax. A return was brought down the other day with regard to the farmers who pay income tax. Only 1,458 farmers pay income tax, or $150,000, all told. I contend that the principle contained in resolution S should be incorporated in resolution 1. There should be equality of treatment as between the urban and the suburban man in connection with payment of these arrears. The time allowed for the payment of the 1942 tax, is not enough; at least there should be a better opportunity to pay this. The farmer is permitted to carry forward for two years any farm losses that there may be, and that principle should be incorporated into resolution 1 and made to apply to industrial workers.
The small industrial workers cannot continue to carry their present burden. The plan may have been all right in theory, but it will not work out in practice. Everybody should pay his proper income tax. There are many farmers who should be paying an income tax. Everybody should pay, not just some. The industrial worker is not in a favoured position; his job is here to-day and gone to-morrow.
They would not adopt this plan in Washington. When I first came to the house I brought up this income tax with the late Mr. Robb, and he was of opinion that we were going too far in taking it all from the municipalities. The municipalities are starved; they cannot carry on with their revenues taken away. How is a man to pay his real estate taxes, his insurance and his mortgage payments all at once, under this budget plan. There are no houses available in Toronto. The soldier coming back from the war cannot get a house. Under tins plan no one will be able to own

Income War Tax
or to buy a house. These added burdens will mean wholesale confiscation of property. I know what I am talking about because I have been connected with municipal affairs for a long time. I know what a hardship it will be for the workers in industry to pay these taxes. I referred to this matter this afternoon. I have great respect for both ministers, but I think they will find it will be impossible for the people to pay these 1942 arrears in the time allowed. They rejected the Ruml plan in the United States. That country does not have a sales tax. Sales tax legislation has been before congress for five or ten years and they have rejected it every year. How is the industrial worker to pay his 1942 and 1943 taxes compounded? I think the ministers have been a little too bashful in connection with publicity. They have a good man in the commissioner of income tax. He comes from Toronto and he knows something about these matters. He is an educated man possessing high talents, but I say to him that I do not think this plan is workable, without further time to pay.
More time should be given to pay these arrears. When a woman is working for $5 or $10 a week, either at domestic work or in a factory, in order to help her husband in keeping their little property, she should not have to pay it all out. Many farm boys and girls have gone to work in munitions plants, and now they are sending out high-school students to take their places. Even the civil service is finding it hard to pay these taxes. It used to be said of Toronto that sixty-four per cent of the people owned their own homes, but now nobody wants to own real estate. They want to get rid of it because they are finding they cannot hold it and the rent control rains property holding. This is simply combining two years' income tax, and it will mean wholesale confiscation of property, because both income taxes and insurance cannot be paid together.
Mortgages will be foreclosed. There are other ways of getting this money. I think the present generation is suffering enough in flesh and blood. This money could be obtained on 1942 arrears by borrowing. If the government is able to borrow at one per cent or less, then at least a better part of these 1942 taxes should be cancelled. That is what should be done instead of promising the people a gold brick. That is all that this resolution 1 is. The people do not understand. We all know of the great publicity which Donald Gordon has and the money which he and his cohorts of advertising people spend on billboard advertising and page ads in the newspapers 72537-123}
and press officials. The minister is too bashful about this; he should spend some of his money on publicity, to let the people know what all this means.
Every person should pay his proper tax. We got into this war and we have to finish it. This form of duplicate taxes is reacting upon the public schools, the separate schools and the high schools and on education as well as on the hospitals. Nobody will have a five-cent piece to spend. How will they be able to pay the different forms of taxes? It cannot be done. More time should be given to pay the 1942 taxes. The people should be given at least six months more, in 1944, to pay. They are so far behind now they will never catch up.
Our soldiers are fighting for $1.30 a day. They find that they cannot hold on to their little pieces of property. Many of their mortgages have been foreclosed. I know of properties which cost $25,000 or $30,000 selling for as low as $7,000. When a man rents his property a tenant may ask for a new furnace or something else, and he is backed up by the force of law and rent control, so that no one wants real estate. Some people have been very heavily fined for technical and minor breaches in the Toronto police courts. They can be fined up to $5,000 by these control people. They have young lawyers handling these cases, many of whom should be at the war. Poor women are being fined $5 or $10 or $100 because they buy half a pound of tea they should not buy.
Let us have equality of treatment for the farmer and the city man under this resolution.. The department should not have touched the Ruml plan at all this year; they should have waited for another year in order to see the results. Canada is the highest taxed country in the world to-day. Great Britain has no sales tax, and yet she is bearing the brunt of the war. She is now receiving fine help from her ally in Washington, but neither Washington nor London has sales taxes. This is all reacting on the people in a way never thought of in the olden days. I do not know how the working classes are going to live. It would have been far better for the war if more time had been devoted on Monday, Tuesday and Wednesday to a discussion of these principles of taxation.
I regret having to make these observations, but I have studied this matter and I know something about the taxation system. The municipalities are simply headed for extinction. The whole constitution will have to be changed to protect provincial and municipal autonomy. They have no revenue; they cannot put up a new door or do a thing. The

Income War Tax
municipalities have been holding down their taxes in a wonderful way. Resolution 1 should be recast and the people given more time to pay these arrears. With the load they are forced to carry the people are worried to death. Talk about freedom from fear; resolution 1 will put more fear into the hearts of the people than anything else I know of. It is worrying the people to death. I know of one man in the constituency of the hon. member for Davenport who died the other day. There are many who cannot make ends meet and are worrying themselves to death as to how to meet taxation. They have been put to extra cost with the heavy winter that has just passed.
The ministers are fine men; they possess many human qualities, and I ask them to give the people more time to pay these 1942 arrears, and at a lower rate of interest.

There seems to be a number of interpretations of resolution 1. So far as investment income is concerned it is clear enough that one-half of the tax shall be paid up to $3,000, but so far as earned income is concerned it is not quite so clear. It would be perfectly clear if it read that the tax on one-half of all the earned income shall be forgiven. May I ask the minister whether "up to $3,000'' has any application so far as earned income is concerned?

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: No, it has not. The $3,000 relates to investment income. Half of the tax on all earned income and up to $3,000 of investment income is forgiven. The rest of the investment income is taxed. There is no forgiveness in respect of that.
So that it matters not whether a man's earned income is $4,000 or $10,000, one-half of the tax is forgiven? Is that correct?

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: That is correct, yes.

May I ask the government if they do not think they would be doing a service to make a national appeal to the provinces and the municipalities against any increased taxation? Many of the men overseas are home owners, and it seems to me that we might give them a more generous greeting when they return home than an increased lax bill. The taxes on homes and real estate in general are now so heavy and the restrictions as to rentals, sales, and improvements are so many, that it would not be unreasonable to have the taxation of municipal property come under the prices board just as so many other things do.
[DOT]

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext:
The government of Canada should be careful not to interfere in the affairs of provinces and municipalities to any greater extent than they feel necessary. I have made it very clear during the last two or three years that this government is most anxious that expenditures by other governments, provincial and municipal, be reduced to the minimum. That is the aspect of the matter which interests me more than the taxation. A reduction in taxation perhaps would follow. It might come anyway as a result of their increasing revenues. I know that some municipalities are reducing their taxes. But I do not know that an appeal from the dominion government to the provinces or to the municipalities not to raise their taxes or to reduce their taxes would be proper. I am most anxious that they keep their expenditures down to the irreducible minimum.
I have an amendment to this resolution, Mr. Chairman, which I should like to place before the committee now. It is as follows:
That resolution No. 1 of the resolutions to amend the Income War Tax Act be amended by adding the words "and trustees taxable on income accumulating for unascertained persons or persons with contingent interests, or income being capitalized in the hands of the trustees" after the word "corporations" in the third line thereof.
How will it read then?

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext:
It will read:
That in respect of the taxation year 1942 the income tax liability, of taxpayers other than corporations and trustees taxable on income accumulating for unascertained persons or persons with contingent interests, or income being capitalized in the hands of the trustees, under subsection 1 of section 9 of the Income War Tax Act, in respect of earned income-
And so on down to the end of the resolution. That makes it clear that there is no forgiveness of any part of the tax on the income of trustees in respect of the income accumulating for unascertained persons or persons with contingent interests, or income being capitalized in the hands of the trustees.
I move accordingly, Mr. Chairman.

By the 1941
act employers were required to deduct the income tax from the earnings of their employees and turn the money over to the government. That has been done in a number of cases. There was also a provision in the act to the effect that this money could be reclaimed in the event of the employee appearing not to be taxable if his earnings were less than $660 per year. In that case the money was to be

Income War Tax
repaid to the employee, provided that the taxpayer applied in. writing for such refund within twelve months from the close of the calendar year in which the amount was collected. There are cases in which the employee did not apply for repayment of this money within the twelve months, and the money is being held by the government. Will the government consider extending the time for repayment of the money so collected so that these employees can have the money that is justly theirs? I say it is theirs because, although the money was deducted from them, they were not taxable, their income being less than $660 for the year. I took the matter up with the officers of the government, and1 they are holding the money up to the present. Will the minister consider extending the time so that these people can get the money that is justly theirs?

That matter has already
received consideration, and a recommendation has been submitted to council that the time be extended so that those who have not submitted their applications for refunds within the twelve months will not be precluded from receiving a refund. An extension of a further six months has been recommended.
Will the minister give me a reply to the observations I have made?

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext:
If the hon. gentleman will
look at what I said last night in introducing this resolution, he will see why we thought that a forgiveness of fifty per cent was the appropriate amount. I understood him to argue to-day that a longer time should be given for payment of the tax, if any, unpaid on the 1942 liability. In a great many cases it is all paid and more than paid, so that there will be refunds from the crown to the taxpayer. In other cases there will be something to be paid by the taxpayer to the crown. The date when the unpaid portion is due is June 30, 1943, when he has to make his returns. He has to pay one-third then, and he has the rest of the year within which to pay the other two-thirds, without interest.

I call to the attention of the minister a return he presented to the effect that income tax is paid in all Canada by only 1,480 farmers, in the total amount of $150,000. Industrial workers and women who do not make any more than many farmers have to pay income tax. Why should the tax not apply to the farmer as well? He has the same income, and he gets protection which is extended to nobody else. I cannot understand why he does not pay income tax.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext:
The farmer is subject to
income tax just as everyone else is.
There is no equality of treatment. It is most unfair.

I am sure that the government does not intend in any event to make a capital levy. But that in effect is what it does under section 3, paragraph (g), of the act, which describes income, in part, as: Annuities or other annual payments received under the provisions of any_ will or trust, irrespective of the date on which such _ will or trust became effective, and notwithstanding that the annuity or annual payments are in whole or in part paid out of capital funds of the estate or trust and whether the same is received in periods longer or shorter than one year.
I should like to know from the minister- and I will ask several questions now, so that he can answer them all at one time-whether consideration should not now be given toward removing that section from the definition of income, because of the anomalous result that those who receive shares from estates in annual amounts are subject in effect to income tax on capital. I believe the point has been raised before, but as yet no satisfactory explanation has been given by the minister as to the reason for that anomalous provision.
Mention was made by the hon. member for Kootenay West (Mr. Esling) of the necessity of something being done on the part of the Minister of Finance (Mr. Ilsley) toward soliciting the cooperation of the provinces not to extend their expenditures during the period of the war. The minister mentioned that he was not concerned with provincial taxation as such, but that he was concerned that provinces should not increase their expenditures. I recently secured a statement showing the expenditures of the provinces, and these statistics prove beyond doubt that during the period of the war every province but one is increasing its expenditure almost by leaps and bounds. I have not yet heard an appeal from the minister to the provinces in respect of this tendency. At the expense of taking up a few minutes I will refer to the expenditures of the

It will be seen that Alberta is the only exception to the general tendency.
The minister has stated that he desires the cooperation of the provinces in keeping down their expenditures, and he has the right to ask for it. Many think to-day that under this modification of the Ruml plan there has been some forgiveness of taxation. I warn the minister that unless he gives a lead to the Canadian people and assures them that the government will see to it that value is received for money spent and that there will not be waste and extravagance, he will have a lot of difficulty.
I think he will agree that where there arc known instances of waste and extravagance they should be eradicated and discontinued at once. If the minister wants to make a success of his victory loan and collect the extra taxation in amount which is being imposed, by reason of the increased rates becoming effective this year, he will have to merchandise the sure knowledge to the people of Canada that waste, where it can be controlled, will end. You can sell the people the idea of sacrifice through taxation if you sell them at the same time the knowledge that needless expenditures will end.
It is not my intention to mention a great many instances of this nature, -but I desire to refer to the salaries paid to officials of the war information board and shown in the return brought down on March 2 in response to a question of the hon. member for Grenville-Dundas (Mr. Casselman). Reading those salaries over, no one can conclude that there is any effective control on the part of the Department of Finance of expenditures which are being made by boards in this country. I will not refer to many of these salaries, because I have other references to make which I wish to bring to the attention of the committee.
First, may I refer to Leo Casey, of the New York office. The information shows that he drew a salary of $13,320.
For doing what?
It states that he was adviser to the wartime information board.
A useless position.
His living allowance is placed at $2,836.05, and his travelling expenses at $748.33.
Nothing short of an outrage.
Then, again in the New York office, S. A. Freifeld, research economist in charge of the news desk, received a salary of $6,660, with travelling expenses of $53.42.
A fourteen-year-old boy could do that.

Next is Mr. H. R. Sutherland, photographic editor from Toronto, who is in charge of distribution of photographs and editorial feature material. His salary is $5,550; living allowance is $2,836.05, and travelling expenses, $440.55. Then, there are others, including J. H. Campbell in charge of the Washington office and its operations. Although he received no salary, his living allowance is placed at $8,103, and his travelling expenses are $427.50.
He must have lived in a royal palace.

Then, J. A. Oastler, assistant to Mr. Campbell, received a salary of $6,327, with living allowances of 83,241.20 and travelling expenses of $734.98. Then there is A. R. Sykes, who supplies information as to Canada's war effort to inquirers at Washington, and by mail to many parts of the United States. His salary is $3,463.20; his living allowances, $2,025.75, and there are no travelling expenses. There are many more very large salaries I could place on record. All the records touching the salaries paid by this board are sealed1 and embalmed in an order for return. In other words, the answer was brought down in such a way that the people generally do not become aware of its existence, except through press items. I repeat that the minister must be able to assure the people of Canada that things such as were revealed in the return I have mentioned shall be discontinued.
I now come to another item in connection with overexpenditures, a matter to which reference has been made within the past few days. I refer to hospitalization at Victoria, British Columbia. The Department of National Defence wished to secure medical accommodation at that point. They were offered the municipally-owned Jubilee hospital, and could have built an additional wing of 250 beds at a cost of $250,000, such sum to be paid by the government. Instead of doing that, the authorities proceeded to build an addition to the naval hospital, to build a new hospital for the air force at Patricia Bay-

On a point of order; is the hon. member in order in discussing this matter, when it could be discussed under an appropriate item in the estimates? Hon. members are anxious to expedite the business before the committee.

speakerposition: Deputy Speaker and Chair of Committees of the Whole of the House of Commons
speechtext:
There is no doubt that the hon. member for Lake Centre is taking a great deal of latitude. I have allowed con-
