siderable latitude throughout the discussion.
It is not my wish to discipline or to attempt to moralize but I hope hon. members will keep as closely as possible to the resolution before the committee.
I shall end it, then, simply by showing the facts.
The resolution we are discussing is, as I understand it, neither a spending nor a taxing resolution. It is an exemption resolution. That being so-
It is a taxing resolution, too.

I trust there may be an appropriate place where my hon. friend can discuss the matters, the discussion of which he has just concluded. I believe, however, we shall make faster progress if we proceed in an orderly fashion.
Let us get ahead with the resolution.

speakerposition: Deputy Speaker and Chair of Committees of the Whole of the House of Commons
speechtext:
I have given my ruling.
I know hon. members will agree when I say that during the years I have been in the house a certain amount of latitude has been allowed in discussions of this kind. I hope and expect that hon. members will not take liberties beyond that. I know they are trying to do all they can to follow the rules.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext:
I do not know whether this point is debatable, nor do I know why I did not raise a point of order earlier. Perhaps it was because I was so much interested in what the hon. member was saying. But I must point out that if under these taxation resolutions the whole field of war expenditures and nonwar expenditures can be discussed, then the rules of order would seem to cease to exercise any restraint. I am afraid that if we do not exercise a little self-discipline, and have that supplemented by the Chair-and I say this respectfully-we shall literally never finish this session. We shall be here twelve months in the year.
Under this resolution the hon. member is speaking about expenditures in Victoria. Then, he was talking about the salaries of employees in New York and Washington. He ingeniously dragged in those matters by saying that if I did not see that these expenditures were cut down I would not collect the taxes. I raised the point the other day that, in connection with another subject, the hon. member's presentation was too artificial and too remote. I am beginning to have a tremendous admiration for his ingenuity, but certainly not for his soundness, if he is seriously advocating that the present discussion is in order.

speakerposition: Deputy Speaker and Chair of Committees of the Whole of the House of Commons
speechtext:
I appreciate what the
minister has said, and I have made my ruling.
I know the committee will realize it is absolutely impossible for me to state definitely where an hon. member should stop. The onus is really put on the individual member to see to it that he stays within the rules. There is no doubt that the hon. member for Lake Centre has been going far afield.

The Minister of
Finance has often asked for examples of overexpenditure, waste and extravagance. I thought I would give him some details; but if the minister does not want them, and if he does not want the assistance I think he should have when putting new taxation into operation, then I will not press the matter.
May I conclude by finishing the reference I was making. I shall not go on to the other examples I have before me. I believe I was pointing out what was done at Victoria, in so far as hospital beds were concerned1. By a course being followed other than that which I think was the proper one the cost to the government was $5,000 a bed, as against $1,000 per bed accommodation.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext:
Mr. Chairman, I rise to a
point of order. I am asking seriously for your ruling as to whether the words the hon. member is now using are in order under this resolution.

speakerposition: Deputy Speaker and Chair of Committees of the Whole of the House of Commons
speechtext:
I must rule that the
words of the hon. member for Lake Centre are not in order under the present discussion.
I should like to know whether or not my question was in order, whether under the head of income a capital levy would in effect be made, under the section that I have mentioned.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: I think that is in order.

Then, I would ask the minister whether consideration will be given to removing that anomaly? It is most unfair to those who years ago were in receipt of capital from an estate payable by annual payments, that that capital should be subject to income tax. I do not know the circumstances under which the section was introduced, but there have been brought to my attention a number of cases in which widows are actually paying income tax upon a share of the deceased husband's estate by reason of this section.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext:
I am informed and believe that the English statute taxes annuities and annual payments. There has been a great deal of litigation as to what that included.
Income War Tax

I believe it does not include term annuities; it does not include annual payments over a particular length of time, one year, two years, three years or anything like that, even though one would think so by reading the section.

Who gave the
interpretation?

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: I am informed that that is the effect of the English decisions, that annuities and annual payments-just in those words-mean annuities and annual payments for life. Our provisions are divided. In the early part of the section there is a provision taxing contractual annuities, those annuities one buys, not term annuities but annuities for life. In that case it may well be argued, as the hon. gentleman has argued, that in the annuity there is a capital element, that part of one's capital is coming back.
Is there any argument to the contrary?

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext:
Oh, yes, certainly, the
English cases are full of it, that w'hen one buys an annuity it is an exchange of a fund for a flow, that one disposes of his capital and takes in return income.

Is there such a provision in the English act as the section to which I refer, 3 (g) ? There is section 3 (b), which refers to annuities or other annual payments received under the provisions of any contract except as in this act otherwise provided. But that is not the section to which I am referring.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: I shall have to get the English act here, so that we shall know what we are talking about. But I was saying that my information is that the English act taxes annuities and annual payments simply, and that we, instead of one section taxing annuities and annual payments, have two subsections: 3 (b), which taxes contractual annuities, and 3 (g), which taxes annuities and annual payments under trusts and wills. The hon. gentleman has spoken about the case of the will. Some cases do arise under that which are hard; there is no doubt about that, and we have given a great deal of consideration to whether we can effect some amendment of section 3 (g). I think I can say it is my intention to introduce some amendment to that section.
This session?

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext:
This session, but it will not go as far as the hon. gentleman urges. He is asking that the tax be removed from annuities and annual payments under wills. We would fMr. Ilsley.]
not do that. But we may go part way, or we may do something about the retroactive feature; I do not know which yet; I have not finished giving consideration to it. But that is not a matter to be dealt with by the resolution. It is not the imposition of a tax; it is relief from taxation, to be dealt with after the resolution is introduced. I shall expect it to be very carefully examined by hon. members, because it is a fairly wide question.

I have just a brief word to say. A year ago I interviewed the Minister of National Revenue in respect of certain criticism which came to me from Fort William as to difficulty in filling in the income tax forms. I wish now to thank him that those whose income is under S3,000 are to get their income tax forms filled in by someone under the minister. This is most commendable because these forms are very difficult to fill in. With all my experience as an accountant I made a mistake of $15 last year, but I made it on the right side and now I am $15 to the good.
I should like also to commend the minister for the pay-as-you-go plan. This is like painless extraction of teeth; you pay your income tax and do not know it, and you have your cheque after it is all over. I thank him for it.

I should like to ask the minister a question relating to resolution 1. Is it possible under this provision that a person who has earned income and investment income, provided that investment income does not exceed $3,000, can be forgiven half of the tax on the total amount?

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: Yes.
Take a hypothetical case. Here is a person with $10,000 earned income and $3,000 investment income, or a total of 813,000; he gets fifty per cent of the whole tax forgiven?

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: Yes.

Whereas a person who
might have $4,000 investment income and nothing more will be forgiven fifty per cent of the tax on only $3,000?

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: That is correct.

It seems rather unfair that a person with $13,000 income is forgiven fifty per cent on the whole amount while another person with only $4,000 income is forgiven fifty per cent on only $3,000. Would the minister explain?

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext:
If the hon. gentleman will look at the budget speech he will see the reason for making a distinction between in-

Income War Tax
vestment income and earned income. One course would be to make no distinction whatever, to forgive half the taxes on all income. We do not want to do that.
Why not?

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: Well, I know my hon. friend would want it.
Not at all; it makes very little difference to me.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext:
We did not want to do that for the reason I cited in the budget speech. Anyone in giving reasons in favour of this plan for forgiving half the tax always puts it on the ground that if something were not done the person earning income would come to a point where he lost his job, or was retired, or died, in which event he would have nothing, or perhaps would have nothing. In a great many cases he would have nothing out of which to pay this large amount of unpaid income tax. That was the ground always put forth as the reason why something should be done to relieve his widow and children from paying perhaps thousands of dollars of income tax, or to relieve him if he had been earning, say $10,000 a year and then went on pension at $4,000 a year, and found himself obliged to pay the full income tax on the $10,000. The same considerations do not apply to the person who has an investment income, because normally the source of his income remains unimpaired whether he retires, whether he loses his job or whether he dies; the source of his income, the capital fund out of which his income is derived, is still there. That is why we made the distinction, and I think it is sound enough. It is not very popular in some quarters, perhaps; nevertheless I think it is sound.
The hon. gentleman has, I think, in mind another distinction, namely, a distinction on the basis of the amount of income. Perhaps this is not so, but from what he says I gather that he would perhaps argue in this way. If you are making a division at $3,000 or $4,000 or $5,000, go by the man's income; make no distinction between investment income and earned income; but forgive, let us say. the tax on incomes up to $3,000, or up to $4,000 or $5,000, and not above that. I gave a great deal of thought to that point, and there was some advocacy of that course of action in the press, though I must say not very much. However, I do not think it is possible to select in regard to earned incomes a line which will have any logic. The higher a man's income, the higher the proportion of the tax that he pays. If a man earning $10,000 were

saddled with his entire income tax and then moved on to a current basis, he would have a terrific load to carry in the year 1943. He would be paying the 1943 tax, and he would be paying the whole of the unpaid1 part, which might be fifty per cent, sixty per cent or seventy per cent, of the 1942 tax. Because he is earning a $10,000 income he is paying at a high rate, and I think it would be simply class legislation to draw a line on the basis of income. However, I think it is sound legislation to draw a line between investment income and earned income on account of the fact I have mentioned, namely, that presumably the source of the investment income is constant. It is there; it is not dissipated; it does not disappear when death, retirement, illness or loss of position takes place.

Apart from the fact that the minister has tried to set aside what I had in mind, I must say that he has stated very clearly the position I felt should be taken in this matter. I take it that he has given this question consideration and has turned it down; nevertheless I should like to press for consideration of this idea, that the forgiving of the tax on fifty per cent of investment income up to S3,000 should apply in cases where that is definitely the only income, but should not apply where the total income of the taxpayer is in the higher brackets, say at whatever figure the minister might arrive at.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: Well, if I am correct in my position that we should make no difference between amounts of earned income, that all earned income is entitled to this concession, then I do not think we should make a difference between combinations. I think then we just have to consider what exemptions we should extend in connection with investment income. There are some persons whose only income is investment income, and who must have some investment income in order to live.

I am not objecting to
the forgiveness in those cases; I am objecting to a man with an earned income of $10,000 getting fifty per cent exemption on that and also getting a fifty per cent exemption on his investment income up to $3,000.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext:
The hon. gentleman would
suggest something else, that as the income went up the $3,000 should go down?
That is right.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: Well, it is worth considering.

I should be glad if the
minister would consider it.

I have a suggestion to offer to the ministers and perhaps to the commissioner with regard to the wording of the resolution, which in its present form has, I think, aroused very natural inquiries such as those put forward by the hon. member for Kootenay West. To make the point perfectly clear, if it were thought worth while I think, if you inserted the words "up to $3,000 in respect of investment income" immediately after the words "in respect of earned income and," you would remove any ambiguity that may exist in the present system. You almost never get to a court in regard to income tax, but you might clarify the resolution and bring it into full accord with the intention which has been made very clear by the minister.
There is another point I wish to mention, and if I am in order I should like to discuss it. I refer to the point raised by the hon. member for Lake Centre, in regard to what the minister called annuity income, which I understood the minister to say could be discussed under this resolution. The minister indicated that careful consideration would be given to perhaps one or both types of so-called annuity incomes. In connection with his giving that consideration may I just point out one case. Take an instance where a father makes a bequest of, say $40,000 as a trust to his executor for the support of his daughter, perhaps an unmarried girl who cannot earn her own living, but instead of having that amount paid to the daughter he creates a trust and leaves it in the hands of his executor to be paid to her at the rate of $2,000 a year. The true character of such a bequest is not income at all; it is a capital lump sum bequest from the father to the daughter. All he does is to defer payment of it to her; but I understand that a recent case was brought to the attention of the very able commissioner in connection with a particular estate, and the ruling has been that under those circumstances this trust of $40,000 in the hands of the executors and paid at the rate of $2,000 a year to the daughter is taxed as though it were income, which means that one-third or more of the $2,000 is taken away from the daughter. The testator never had any such intention. That is not income at all; it is capital, purely and simply. I suggest that the minister might give serious consideration to that problem, because under the rulings that have been made with regard to the present wording of the act I understand this $2,000 is taxed as the income of an unmarried person, as though it were pure income.

Mr. ILSLEY; I am told that in such a case, if there were a bequest to a daughter and her heirs of $2,000 a year until the fund was exhausted, that would not be regarded as an annuity or as annual payments. If $40,000 were the amount, it would be a $40,000 bequest payable to the daughter at $2,000 a year irrespective of her death, and would not be taxable as an annuity under the English cases. However, if it went on to her death, then it would be an annuity.

I appreciate that definition. My information was that in a given case the ruling had been that it was still treated as income. If I am wrong in that, then the matter does not need curing.
Progress reported.
